title: Jonah sulks (Jonah 3–4)
hook: the enemy city repents and Jonah is furious that God is merciful

segments.voice: Yesterday, Jonah ran west, went down and down, and prayed from inside the great fish. Your line was you can't outrun him. What step did you take toward your Nineveh? Day four hundred thirty.

The fish puts Jonah out on dry land, and the word of the Lord comes to him a second time, exactly the same: arise, go to Ninive. This time he goes. Ninive is enormous, a three days' walk across, the text says. Jonah walks one day in and preaches a sermon of one sentence. In the Douay-Rheims: "Yet forty days, and Ninive shall be destroyed." That's all of it. No call to repent. No promise. No mention of mercy. And the city whose wickedness, God said, had come up before him, believes him.
screen: `THE SAME WORD, A SECOND TIME.` → `A SERMON OF ONE SENTENCE.` → `THE CITY BELIEVES.`

segments.voice: The people proclaim a fast and put on sackcloth, from the greatest to the least. The news reaches the king, and he gets up from his throne, takes off his robe, and sits in ashes. He decrees that nobody eat, not even the oxen and the sheep; the animals wear sackcloth too. Who knows, he says, whether God will turn and forgive. And God sees what they did, how they turned from their evil way, and doesn't bring the destruction. A prophet's warning, heard at once, from the king down to the cattle. And Jonah is furious. Then he admits why he ran in the first place. I knew it, he says. I knew you are a gracious and merciful God, patient, rich in compassion, ready to forgive. Those are God's own words about himself from Exodus, and Jonah throws them back like a complaint. He'd rather die. God asks one quiet question: do you think you have reason to be angry? Jonah goes out east of the city to watch, hoping. God makes a plant grow over him for shade, and Jonah is very glad of it. Nobody knows what plant it was. The King James says a gourd; Jerome's Latin, and so the Douay, says ivy. When Jerome's new translation reached a church in North Africa, Augustine reported that the congregation nearly rioted over the change. Then a worm kills the plant, a scorching wind blows, and Jonah wants to die again. And God says: you grieve over a plant you didn't plant or grow. Should I not spare Nineveh, that great city, with more than a hundred and twenty thousand people who can't tell their right hand from their left, and many beasts? And the book ends. On the question. Jonah never answers.
screen: `EVEN THE OXEN WEAR SACKCLOTH.` · `I KNEW YOU WERE MERCIFUL.` · `A GOURD, OR IVY? NOBODY KNOWS.` · `THE BOOK ENDS ON A QUESTION.` · then, large: `SHOULD I NOT SPARE NINEVEH?`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: be glad at someone's second chance. Settle, and breathe. Think of someone who got a second chance you're not sure they deserved. A sibling who always gets forgiven. A colleague who messed up and got promoted anyway. A public figure who apologized. Notice the sulk, if there is one, the little part of you sitting east of the city, hoping for fire. Don't scold it. Just let God's question sit next to it: should I not spare them? Then see if you can be glad, even a little. If you pray, you can pray for them by name. The bell holds the time.
Jonah sulks. The prophet whose one-sentence sermon saved an enemy city, and who sat outside it, angry that God was merciful. Today's word.
Your line: should I not spare them. Today, when someone gets a second chance, say something kind about it, out loud, to someone. Day four hundred thirty.

howItsDone: Catholics hear Nineveh's repentance read at Mass in Lent, and the Church holds up the Ninevites' fasting and sackcloth as a picture of the penance of the Lenten season.

fork.setup: you're Jonah. you preached destruction, and the whole enemy city repented. God spared them. what do you do?
options: throw a party with the Ninevites.
get angry, and sit outside the city hoping it burns anyway.
fork.reveal: he's furious, and says why he ran: he knew God was gracious and merciful. he sits east of the city to watch.

original.note: Hebrew: Jonah's plant. nobody knows what it was; translations have gourd, ivy or castor-oil plant.

trapdoor: what you thought: Jonah's story ends when the fish spits him out.
what it means: the second half is the harder story: a prophet angry that God forgave his enemies, and God asking him to care.
what a scholar hears: Jonah quotes God's self-description from Exodus 34:6 as a complaint; and the book ends on an unanswered question, aimed at the reader.

sources.quoted: Yet forty days, and Ninive shall be destroyed.

notes: Editor review (2026-10-01): cut the superlatives ('the shortest sermon in the Bible', 'the most successful sermon any prophet ever preached', 'the most wicked city') and the uncited Hebrew word count ('five words') from the voice, screen, word, match and myth.
Douay-Rheims wording of Jonas 3:4 quoted from memory; please check.
'Five words in Hebrew' ('od arba'im yom ve-Nineveh nehpakhet): confirm the count.
Augustine's Letter 71 reports the disturbance at Oea over Jerome's 'hedera' (ivy) for 'cucurbita' (gourd); Jerome replies in Letter 112. 'Nearly rioted' paraphrases 'tumult'. Confirm.
'The most successful sermon any prophet ever preached' is the writer's light comment, not a textual claim; soften if a Keeper prefers.
